title: In 1917 San Francisco opened what was then the world’s longest streetcar tunnel

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still from 1917: a crowd in hats and long coats stands beside an arched tunnel portal as a streetcar goes in.

body: In the early 1900s much of San Francisco’s west side, beyond the Twin Peaks hills, was still undeveloped. One supporter of a tunnel complained in 1909 that 40,000 San Franciscans lived across the bay or in San Mateo County because transit was so poor. Work began in December 1914, the crews digging from both ends met on 5 April 1917, and the **Twin Peaks Tunnel**, 2.27 miles (3.65 km) long, was dedicated that July. The western districts it would open up were assessed 85% of the cost, and the tunnel still carries Muni Metro trains today.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film: a huge crowd fills a street on a hillside; then, at an arched tunnel portal, a streetcar rolls past the waiting crowd and into the tunnel.
slides.caption: Opening celebrations, 1917: crowds pack the street, then a streetcar rolls past onlookers into the arched tunnel portal.

events.text: Crews from each end break through

slides.heading: The western districts were assessed 85% of the tunnel’s cost
slides.note: The western assessment area covered about 4,000 acres.

slides.question: Who drove the first fare-paying streetcar through the tunnel in 1918?
slides.explanation: Mayor James Rolph acted as motorman. Most of the paying passengers were city supervisors, their wives and invited guests, and the trip took seven minutes.

slides.label: below the surface at Forest Hill station, inside the tunnel
slides.text: It was first called Laguna Honda. The tunnel’s ventilation shaft goes down 110 feet.
